clue.text: Correctionsbush could make to take a decisive step

indicators.note: the letters of the run-together words could be made into something else, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the page runs 'Corrections' and 'bush' together; their fifteen letters are the fodder

explanation.surface: A political pundit says owning up to errors is the bold move a US president named Bush could make.
explanation.walkthrough: The scanned clue runs 'Corrections' and 'bush' together; 'could make' rearranges all fifteen letters. Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon river committed him to civil war.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar's crossing of that river into Italy was an irrevocable act, so the phrase means committing oneself past the point of no return.

clue.text: Defences come down, honour finally yielding, having these?

definitions.text: Defences come down, honour finally yielding, having these?

indicators.note: yielding means giving up, so the letter named is surrendered from the defences

parts.note: suits of armour are defences, so the plural is armours

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word honour

explanation.surface: A coy figure lowers their guard and gives up their virtue in a romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ARMOURS and let the R at the end of 'honour' go; the whole clue then describes love affairs, where defences and honour both give way.
explanation.definitionFit: Love affairs are romances in which guards are lowered and virtue may be surrendered, as the whole clue pictures.

clue.text: Contents of these could appear in latrines

indicators.note: the word latrines could be rearranged so that another word shows up in its letters

explanation.surface: Something unpleasant might turn up in a public toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could appear in' rearranges LATRINES; the definition 'Contents' plays on what bowels hold and on where their contents end up.
explanation.definitionFit: Guts or innards are the inner contents of a body.

clue.text: What could modify strands reworking Lord of the Rings

indicators.note: reworking a title means remaking it, so the letters of the title are rearranged

explanation.surface: A screenwriter's adaptation of Tolkien's epic changes some storylines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strands' looks like plot threads in a film, but here it means beaches; the movement of sand along the coast reshapes them.
explanation.definitionFit: This coastal process carries sand and shingle along beaches, gradually reshaping a strand, an old word for shore.

clue.text: Your old lab animals taken short-to do with glands

parts.note: thy is the archaic form of your

indicators.note: taken short means cut off before the end, so the last letter of the word is lost

parts.note: mice are the classic laboratory animals

explanation.surface: Archaic phrasing about a researcher's rodents, followed by a medical note on glands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken short' drops the last letter of MICE to leave MIC.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective refers to the thymus, a gland in the chest that helps develop immune cells.

clue.text: One improvising a gardening tool involving end of trowel

indicators.note: involving means taking something in, so the dibber wraps round the extra letter

parts.note: a dibber is a pointed tool for making holes to plant seeds or bulbs

indicators.note: end of points to the final letter of the word trowel

explanation.surface: Someone improvises a garden tool with a trowel's tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts the L at the end of 'trowel' inside DIBBER, after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: An extemporiser speaks or performs off the cuff, without preparation.

clue.text: She raises charges to enter profession

definitions.text: She raises charges to enter profession

parts.words: She raises charges to enter profession
parts.note: reads like a woman levying fees for joining a trade, but 'charges' are pupils she prepares for working life

explanation.surface: A woman sets fees for anyone wanting to join a profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raises charges' suggests billing; in fact a school's careers adviser brings up her pupils (her charges) ready for jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A female teacher who advises pupils on jobs helps them into working life.

clue.text: Latin men turned crazy

indicators.note: turned means flipped round, so the letters for men are read backwards

parts.note: OR (other ranks) means enlisted men in the army
manic means wildly frenzied, crazy

explanation.surface: Italian men went mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses OR, the military abbreviation for other ranks, giving RO before MANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes languages descended from the speech of ancient Rome, so it means derived from that tongue.

clue.text: Business presenting a bill for Congress

definitions.text: Business presenting a bill for Congress

parts.words: Business presenting a bill for Congress
parts.note: a bill for Congress looks like legislation sent to the US legislature, but here it is an invoice for sexual congress

explanation.surface: A lobbying firm drafts legislation for the US legislature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' is capitalised to suggest the US legislature, but means sexual intercourse; the 'bill' is the charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that supplies prostitutes charges clients for sex, an escort business.

clue.text: Old Greek character with help put back snakes

parts.note: phi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

indicators.note: put back means set in reverse order, so the letters for help run backwards

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek figure with an assistant who restored some snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' reverses the word for help; 'character' suggests a person in a Greek drama but means a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the zoological name for the serpent suborder, so it covers all snakes.

clue.text: I'm super resolving about dispute with run out, say

definitions.text: I'm super resolving about dispute with run out, say

indicators.note: about means going round, so the rearranged letters surround the rest
resolving means breaking into parts and settling anew, so the letters are rearranged
R is the cricket abbreviation for run, and out says that letter leaves the word

parts.note: a quarrel is a dispute
eg, for example, is what say means

explanation.surface: A cricket official boasts of settling a row over a contested run-out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolving' rearranges I'M SUPER into S...UMPIRE, which goes 'about' QUAREL (QUARREL with one R, the cricket run, 'out') plus EG. The cricket umpire at square leg judges run-outs, so the whole clue is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The official standing at the side of the pitch in cricket rules on run-outs at the batter's end.

clue.text: Hearten big Scots performing this

indicators.note: performing means putting on a show, and here the letters of the phrase put on a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Cheer on large Scotsmen as they compete at the Highland games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'performing' rearranges HEARTEN BIG SCOTS; the whole clue describes the Highland games event, a Scottish athletics contest of flinging a tree trunk end over end.
explanation.definitionFit: Throwing a long wooden pole end over end is a Highland games event for strong Scotsmen.

clue.text: Recipient of product ensured changes

indicators.note: changes means alters, so the letters of ensured are reordered

explanation.surface: Making sure a product reaches its buyer brings changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges ENSURED.
explanation.definitionFit: The consumer is the person who ultimately uses a product once it has passed through the supply chain.

clue.text: Old TV show — pop star has no time for me

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father, dad

indicators.note: T is the abbreviation for time, and has no says it is dropped from the word

parts.note: taken as the word star
in colloquial British speech 'me' stands for my, as in 'me mum'

explanation.surface: A father who was once famous is no longer willing to spend time on his child.
explanation.walkthrough: DAD'S ARMY is a classic BBC sitcom (1968-77) about the Home Guard. 'has no time' takes T from STAR to leave SAR; 'me' gives MY as in British colloquial speech.
explanation.definitionFit: This BBC sitcom about the wartime Home Guard first aired in the 1960s, so it is a vintage television programme.

clue.text: Stage to provide backing or play guitar

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the little word or is read backwards

parts.note: to strum is to play a guitar by sweeping the strings

explanation.surface: A musician offers either to sing backing vocals or to play guitar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' looks like musical accompaniment in this guitar picture, but it is the reversal signal for 'or'.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised platform for a speaker or conductor is a kind of stage.

clue.text: What spread word of gas privatisation in Devon?

definitions.text: What spread word of gas privatisation in Devon?

parts.words: What spread word of gas privatisation in Devon?
parts.note: the 1986 British Gas sell-off was advertised with the slogan 'If you see Sid, tell him', so word spread from the lips of that imaginary Sid; split another way it is a seaside town in Devon

explanation.surface: Asks who told people in a West Country county about the selling-off of the gas industry.
explanation.walkthrough: The British Gas share sale was promoted by 'Tell Sid' adverts; read in two parts the answer is Sid plus the organ of speech. Devon is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaside resort on the south Devon coast, whose name splits into a man's name and the organ that speaks.

clue.text: Liable to lead to difference between left and right, being short staffed

definitions.text: Liable to lead to difference between left and right, being short staffed

parts.words: Liable to lead to difference between left and right, being short staffed
parts.note: a preference for one hand over the other is what makes left and right differ, and being short of hands (staff) is the other reading; together they suggest a word for deceitfulness

explanation.surface: A shortage of staff threatens to split left from right.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on 'handedness' (left- or right-hand preference) and 'under-handed' (short of hands, workers); the real sense is sly deceit.
explanation.definitionFit: Slyness or deceit, the quality of acting secretly and dishonestly, here reached through jokes about hands and staffing.

clue.text: Rush endlessly around place standing

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the cut-down plant goes round the word for place
endlessly means without its end, so the final letter of the plant is dropped

parts.note: a rush is a reed, a marsh plant
to put something is to place it

explanation.surface: Someone hurries around a spot where they are standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rush' looks like a verb meaning hurry, but it is the marsh plant; 'endlessly' trims its last letter and 'around' wraps the result round the word for place.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing in the sense of reputation is how highly someone is regarded.

clue.text: Feature of big swing song providing finale

definitions.meaning: big band swing numbers are known for a rousing climactic close
the last part of a show or piece

explanation.walkthrough: 'providing' is a link between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclusion is both the climax a swing number builds to and the finale of any work.

clue.text: Pale pipe could be arranged so tidily

indicators.note: so means in this way, telling the solver to set the rearranged pipe within the phrase for arranged

parts.note: arranged means set in order, tidy

indicators.note: could be says the words pale pipe could become something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tidies their pipes by colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges PALE PIPE, and the result sits inside the phrase that 'arranged' gives; 'so' loosely signals that placing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means perfectly neat and orderly, as in a spotless room.

clue.text: Sort of pressure created by very big annual test in class primarily

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, very big
the MOT is the yearly roadworthiness test for British cars

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letters of the next two words are taken

explanation.surface: Pupils feel the strain of a huge yearly exam in class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'annual test' sounds like a school exam but is the MOT, the yearly check British cars must pass; OS (outsize) is clothing shorthand for very big.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of pressure arises when a solvent passes through a membrane between solutions of different concentration.

clue.text: Disease in which muscle spasms and tautens painfully

definitions.text: Disease in which muscle spasms and tautens painfully

indicators.note: painfully suggests something twisted and contorted, so the letters of tautens are rearranged

explanation.surface: Describes an illness that makes muscles contract and tighten in agony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'painfully' rearranges TAUTENS; the whole clue also describes the disease, also called lockjaw.
explanation.definitionFit: This bacterial infection causes rigid muscle spasms, notably of the jaw.
